summary.text: The mixed layer is a layer of an ocean or lake in which active turbulence has stirred a range of depths until temperature and salinity are nearly uniform.
Because seawater holds far more heat than air, the top 2.5 m of the ocean stores as much heat as the entire atmosphere above it.
Its depth sets how much light marine life receives, so when it turns shallow in spring there is often a bloom of phytoplankton.

facts.label: Heat in top 2.5 m
facts.value: As much as the entire atmosphere above

facts.label: Deepest mixed layers
facts.value: Over 2000 m, in places like the Labrador Sea

facts.label: Marker of its bottom
facts.value: Often a sharp temperature change, the thermocline

items.prompt: In the North Atlantic winter, the mixed layer deepens a great deal. What happens to the tiny drifting algae near the surface?

options.label: They thrive on the extra stirring
They get too little light, and chlorophyll drops
They sink and turn into ocean sediment
They are unaffected by how deep it gets

items.explain: In very deep mixed layers phytoplankton cannot get enough light, so winter deepening brings a strong fall in surface chlorophyll a.

items.prompt: Seawater stores far more heat than air does. The top 2.5 m of the ocean holds about as much heat as what?

options.label: The air in a large city
The lowest kilometre of air
A single summer thunderstorm
The whole atmosphere above it

items.explain: Because the specific heat of ocean water is much larger than that of air, the top 2.5 m holds as much heat as the entire atmosphere above.

items.prompt: On a cold night the surface water cools until it is denser than the water just below. What happens next?

options.label: It sinks, and convection stirs the layer
It stays on top as a cold, still lid
It rises higher and then evaporates
It spreads sideways without mixing

items.explain: When cooling raises surface density, convection occurs; this process forms the deepest mixed layers.

items.prompt: Breaking waves pump a great deal of energy into the top few meters of the sea. Why doesn't that energy stir the water very deep?

options.label: Salt in the water absorbs the energy
Waves only move water sideways
Most of it dissipates quite rapidly
Fish swimming below cancel it out

items.explain: Wave-driven turbulence injects a lot of energy into the upper few meters, but most of it dissipates relatively rapidly.

items.prompt: An oceanographer finds the bottom of the mixed layer by noting where temperature first differs from the surface by a set amount. Why does this work?

options.label: Temperature rises steadily all the way down
Light vanishes exactly at that depth
Currents come to a full stop at that depth
The layer is nearly uniform, then changes at its base

items.explain: The mixed layer is nearly uniform in temperature and salinity, and its bottom is marked by a gradient where water properties change.

items.prompt: Inside the mixed layer, temperature and salinity barely vary from top to bottom. What can still change sharply within it?

options.label: Salinity
Temperature
Current speed
Freezing point

items.explain: Although properties like temperature and salinity are nearly uniform, velocities may show significant shears within the mixed layer.
